overview: Early Slavic communities is a cautious name for varied groups across eastern, central, and southeastern Europe between about 500 and 800 CE. It does not name one state, bounded people, uniform archaeological culture, or direct ancestor of a modern nation. Byzantine and Latin writers began using Sclaveni, Antes, and Wends in the sixth and seventh centuries, usually for frontiers, raids, diplomacy, or war. Linguists reconstruct Proto-Slavic; archaeologists compare settlements, pottery, tools, food remains, and graves; geneticists study sampled bodies. These records answer different questions and cannot collapse into one ethnicity. Communities farmed, kept animals, worked iron, moved, traded, or lived under Avar and neighboring rulers. Regional coalitions appeared, including Samo's, without uniting all Slavic speakers. The atlas polygon exists only at 700 and covers a coarse central-European footprint while giving nearby places to Czechs, Moravians, Polanes, Kryvichs, Severians, Avars, and others. It is an editorial layer, not an ancient frontier. By 800, diverse regional communities and polities make the umbrella card a transformation rather than a vanished nation.

periods.title: 500 to 540: evidence before a stable label
periods.summary: Archaeologists identify settlements and artifact traditions across broad regions, while linguists reconstruct speech history indirectly. Contemporary sources do not yet provide a clear, self-authored Slavic collective account. This opening boundary is a teaching convention and cannot locate one homeland, founding generation, or ethnically uniform population.

periods.title: 540 to 570: Sclaveni and Antes in imperial texts
periods.summary: Sixth-century Byzantine and Gothic writers made Sclaveni and Antes visible while describing the Danube frontier, warfare, and diplomacy. Their labels matter, but they are outsider categories shaped by literary purpose. Pottery distributions and reconstructed language must be compared with those texts rather than treated as automatic translations of them.

periods.title: 570 to 600: Avar rule and regional movement
periods.summary: After Avar power entered the Carpathian Basin, some Slavic-speaking communities lived under Avar authority, others cooperated in campaigns, and still others remained beyond direct control. Sparse Greek, Latin, and eastern sources leave local arrangements uncertain. One frontier history cannot stand for communities from the Baltic to the Balkans.

periods.title: 600 to 630: settlements and contacts widen
periods.summary: Settlements with early Slavic-associated pottery appeared across the Eastern Alps and Pannonia in regionally different sequences. Radiocarbon dates refine older culture-historical narratives, while contacts with Avars, Lombards, Byzantines, and local populations complicate any replacement story. Houses and pots mark practices, not a census of spoken language.

periods.title: 630 to 660: Samo in a Frankish narrative
periods.summary: Fredegar describes a coalition associated with Samo amid conflict involving Wends, Avars, and Franks. The chronicle is the main narrative and uses ethnic and political terms strategically. It documents organized action in one western zone, not the birth of a universal Slavic kingdom or a reliable map of Samo's borders.

periods.title: 660 to 700: long-lived settlements, changing households
periods.summary: Roztoky accumulated hundreds of house traces over generations rather than holding every building at once. Charcoal, sediment, and plant evidence help reconstruct fuel and environment, while abandonment processes complicate room-by-room stories. Regional settlement growth does not prove one government, one migration route, or a standardized household plan.

periods.title: 700 to 750: regional communities become clearer
periods.summary: Archaeologists distinguish Early Hillfort and other regional phases, but cremation leaves major gaps in ancient-DNA sampling. Burials, settlements, pottery, and later genomes illuminate different populations at different dates. The atlas's single 700 polygon therefore simplifies a landscape already divided by local histories and neighboring powers.

periods.title: 750 to 800: aggregation and frontier change
periods.summary: By the late eighth century, fortified centers, elite networks, Avar decline, and Carolingian pressure altered parts of Central Europe. Contacts with writing existed, but durable Slavic literary culture belongs mainly after 800. Regional institutions were forming unevenly, so the broad Early Slavic umbrella closes through differentiation rather than collective collapse.

sections.title: Exact identity, chronology, and atlas geometry

items.text: The exact id is proto-slavs, indexed as Early Slavs with the alias Proto-Slavs, a culture dated approximately 700 to 800. No exact card, card-index association, or researched override exists. This packet renames the subject Early Slavic communities and expands the historical teaching interval to circa 500 to 800.

All fifty border snapshots were audited. The exact id occurs once, only in world-700.json, as one Polygon with one component, two rings, and 132 positions. Coverage reports the same single interval and border-file count. The inner ring is geometry structure, not evidence for an excluded ancient people.

The decoded polygon spans roughly 7.51 to 29.10 degrees east and 47.27 to 55.10 degrees north. Its planar exterior centroid lies near 18.51 east and 51.16 north. These values describe the atlas drawing only; they are not a capital, homeland center, demographic average, or surveyed frontier.

At 700, Krakow, Lubeck, and the center probe fall inside the target. Prague is owned by Czechs; Mikulcice and Bratislava by Moravians; Warsaw by Polanes; Kyiv by Severians; Novgorod by Kryvichs; Belgrade by Avars. Gdansk is unowned. This mosaic contradicts any single-state reading.

The target shares one topology arc each with Avars, Frisians, Saxons, the Frankish kingdom, Czechs, Moravians, Polanes, and Balts, without measured area overlaps. At 800 and 900, new owners and overlapping layers replace it. Those editorial changes cannot establish conquest, descent, or named historical successors.

sections.title: Sources, movement, and the limits of labels

items.text: Ancient DNA supports substantial movement from eastern Europe during the sixth to eighth centuries, with sharply different outcomes between regions. It strengthens a migration component without turning genes into language, culture, or identity. Sampled burials cannot tell researchers what each person called themselves or which language they spoke.

Some regions show replacement on a large scale; others show integration with existing populations. That variation matters more than a single migration arrow. Archaeological styles, outsider ethnonyms, reconstructed Proto-Slavic, and genomic ancestry overlap imperfectly, so each line of evidence must retain its own dates, places, and uncertainties.

Earlier archaeology often treated pottery types as direct ethnic maps and projected modern Slavic nations deep into prehistory. Historiographic review shows how those methods served competing national stories. A Prague-type vessel can help date a context, but it cannot disclose the potter's language, ancestry, loyalty, or passport.

Cremation was common in many early Slavic-associated settings, leaving fewer unburned bodies for genome analysis. The Moravian genomic record therefore becomes clearer in later burial phases than in the crucial sixth and seventh centuries. Genetic conclusions must follow the surviving sample rather than fill its chronological gap by assumption.

Procopius described Sclaveni and Antes through an imperial frontier lens and famously contrasted leaders with collective decision making. Modern analysis warns against converting his literary contrast into a constitution for every settlement. Texts reveal encounters and authorial categories; they do not provide minutes from a village assembly.

More than 300 sunken houses were partly or fully excavated at sixth- to seventh-century Roztoky. Stone ovens and posthole patterns survive where wood does not. The assemblage reveals repeated building choices, but the houses accumulated over time and should not be reconstructed as one enormous town occupied on a single afternoon.

Prague-type houses are often square, single-room, semi-sunken buildings with a stone oven in one corner. Their association with the archaeological horizon is strong but not absolute across every region. A familiar house form records learned construction practice; it does not prove identical household size, kinship, wealth, or ethnicity.

House fills preserve abandonment and later deposition as well as activity during occupation. Soil, postholes, oven stones, and ecofacts must be read together before assigning a room's use. A seed in a filled pit may document cooking, sweeping, dumping, animal disturbance, or later erosion rather than its last supper.

Charcoal and micromorphology at Roztoky help reconstruct woodland use, fuel selection, and how sunken buildings filled after abandonment. Estimates of hundreds of structures over roughly 120 to 150 years emphasize turnover. A house count is therefore a settlement biography, not a simultaneous population total.

Excavations at Nova Tabla examined 189 early medieval structures and separated settlement horizons spanning the sixth to early ninth centuries. Radiocarbon dates and pottery sequences reveal change near the Eastern Alps. The regional record joins a wider story without supplying a uniform calendar for every Slavic-speaking community.

sections.title: Food, farming, animals, and daily work

items.text: Chemical and isotopic work in Moravia and Lower Austria places Slavic-associated changes in housing, pottery, and foodways by 598 at the latest, probably between about 560 and 590. The convergence of dates and practices is stronger than typology alone, while still describing particular studied sites rather than all regions.

Lipid residues in pottery support cooking millet porridge with milk and possibly processing honey or beeswax. Millet also dominates archaeobotanical evidence at Roztoky and several Moravian settlements. These results make everyday meals visible, but one absorbed residue cannot identify the cook, serving group, recipe name, or festive occasion.

Some vessels held mixtures consistent with soups, stews, dairy, or meat processing. Isotopes and plant remains broaden the dietary picture beyond one signature food. Communities chose crops and animals within local soils, climates, and contacts, so millet's importance should not become another ethnic badge stamped onto every cooking pot.

Upper Tisza settlements preserve indirect evidence for agriculture, domestic crafts, tools, and iron utensils, with possible limited specialization. Farming, animal care, repair, and food preparation required coordinated seasonal labor. The evidence identifies tasks more securely than it assigns them permanently by sex, age, rank, or household status.

Sediments from the Pohansko well preserve plant use, animal husbandry, flooding, and later waste within a seventh- to eighth-century settlement. Such mixed deposits show how water, livestock, food, and discard crossed paths. They illuminate ordinary work without turning every seed, bone, or muddy footprint into a separate occupation.

Multigenerational pedigrees in one eastern German Slavic-period region suggest local male lines, women moving between communities, avoidance of close-kin unions, and occasionally multiple reproductive partners. These are powerful household clues from sampled cemeteries. The study explicitly finds regional differences, so they are not universal rules for Early Slavic families.

Roztoky houses changed, burned, were abandoned, and filled over generations. Their single rooms may have hosted sleeping, food preparation, craft, storage, and visiting, but floor plans do not name residents. Archaeologists should test household membership with activity traces, burial, and biomolecular evidence rather than assume one nuclear family per structure.

Tools and production debris show tasks that could be shared, taught, or specialized within and between households. They rarely preserve the worker's age or gender. Social life included cooperation and dependency, yet a spindle, knife, or slag fragment should not be used as an automatic identity tag for its last user.

Cremation transforms and fragments bodies, complicating age, disease, kinship, and grave reconstruction. Scientific analysis can compare burning intensity and pyre management, while precise family relationships often remain unavailable. A shared cemetery may express community, locality, ritual, or alliance; it is not automatically a biological family plot.

Early leaders, war bands, assemblies, and negotiated coalitions could coexist. Procopius's language about democracy does not require equal power, fixed voting rules, or leaderless villages, just as named leaders do not establish hereditary monarchies everywhere. Political authority varied with region, conflict, wealth, age, and external relationships.

Children likely learned through participation in farming, animal care, pottery, building, food preparation, and repair. These tasks demanded memory, observation, practice, and correction. Archaeology supports skill transmission but does not identify a standard school, classroom, curriculum, or age of graduation for communities between 500 and 800.

At Nova Tabla, handmade pottery fabrics, surface treatment, firing, and vessel form changed within closely dated horizons. Such technical sequences preserve choices transmitted between makers. They can suggest communities of practice and learners, but finished pots seldom reveal whether instruction came from parents, other relatives, neighbors, itinerant specialists, or experimentation.

A cattle rib from Lany, dated around 600, carries six legible Elder Futhark runes from the end of an alphabet sequence, with two expected signs omitted. Uneven carving and repeated strokes support a writing exercise. The carver's identity and spoken language remain unknown, so the object records contact, not Slavic literacy.

Before the ninth century, rare inscribed objects show encounters with writing rather than a widespread educational system. The Lany exercise may reflect person-to-person teaching, while later churches and elites supported sustained literacy. No evidence establishes that ordinary children in sixth- to eighth-century settlements attended formal lessons or copied texts.

Old Church Slavonic is the earliest documented Slavic language, but its literary period begins around the mid-ninth century. It is a South Slavic literary language, not Proto-Slavic written down unchanged. Its manuscripts cannot be moved backward to provide eighth-century schoolbooks, spelling exercises, or household reading practices.

At Borovce, enamel hypoplasia in an eighth- to early twelfth-century skeletal series records episodes when childhood tooth growth was disrupted. Possible causes include disease, nutrition, and interacting environmental stress. The lesion is evidence of physiological interruption, not a single diagnosis, named epidemic, or measure of one person's suffering.

Borovce begins within this card's final century but continues long afterward. Its reported frequencies therefore cannot describe all communities from 500 to 800. The study offers a comparative window into childhood stress and survival while demonstrating why broad atlas labels should not receive one universal disease rate.

Croatian skeletal series preserve caries, tooth loss, abscesses, calculus, resorption, and wear across a seventh- to eleventh-century composite sample. Teeth can connect food processing and oral health, but the chronology extends beyond this card and combines sites. Regional dental patterns must remain comparisons, not a pan-Slavic medical chart.

Sipar's sixth- to eighth-century cemetery contained eighteen infants under eighteen months, many with skeletal changes consistent with serious physiological stress. Preliminary ancestry results place most in a wider Mediterranean context. The cemetery is valuable regional evidence about infant vulnerability, but it cannot be relabeled as a representative Early Slavic nursery.

No consulted source preserves an Early Slavic medical manual, prescription, named healer, or standardized treatment from 500 to 800. Healing and care may be inferred cautiously when people survived injury or illness, but bones chiefly record outcomes. Remedies, caregiving relationships, symptoms, pain, and bedside decisions usually remain unknown.

Early Slavic expansion involved three recurring ways of securing water: settlement along streams, use of natural springs, and dependence on hand-dug wells. These strategies fit dispersed rural landscapes and varied local geology. They should not be combined into a single engineered network or attributed to one central water authority.

Historical water vocabulary records borrowing and contact as well as inherited terms. Linguistic evidence can suggest when communities encountered particular landscapes or neighbors, but it does not locate every spring archaeologically. Words and wells strengthen each other only when chronology and geography align; neither should silently repair gaps in the other.

The Pohansko well was used and filled during the seventh and eighth centuries. Its stratified sediments record construction, maintenance, abandonment, flooding, and discard. A well was therefore both infrastructure and a changing place in settlement life, not merely a timeless blue circle added to an archaeological plan.

Plant remains, animal evidence, chemical markers, and sediments in the Pohansko well document husbandry and waste management around the settlement. Once abandoned, wells could receive runoff and refuse. That history warns against assuming everything recovered from a water shaft entered while residents were drawing clean drinking water.

The consulted settlement studies securely document ovens, pits, streams, springs, and wells, but they do not establish standardized household toilets, latrines, sewers, or municipal refuse collection across Early Slavic communities. Sanitation is best described through water access, sweeping, dumping, drainage, and feature reuse where evidence survives.

Early Prague-type pottery was commonly handmade, porous, and initially undecorated; forms and finishing changed during the seventh century at Nova Tabla. Makers selected clay, temper, forming methods, and firing conditions. Those decisions record technical knowledge and local adaptation without requiring a centralized pottery industry or one ethnic recipe.

Upper Tisza evidence links farming settlements with domestic craft and production of tools and iron utensils. Some work may have involved specialists, although workshop organization remains uncertain. Iron objects depended on ore, fuel, smelting, forging, repair, and exchange, connecting humble household needs to knowledge extending beyond one dwelling.

Multiple Slavic words for smiths developed around the expansion period, while archaeology traces uneven adoption of iron-working traditions. Language and slag together suggest contact and integration into established Central European metal economies. Neither proves that every settlement smelted ore, that every smith spoke Proto-Slavic, or that technology caused migration.

Secure Slavic-language writing sample for 500 to 800: status, absent. Language, script, original text, transliteration, translation, date, author, and attribution are unavailable. Proto-Slavic is reconstructed rather than directly attested, and Old Church Slavonic literary evidence begins later. Supplying an invented greeting or prayer would erase this evidentiary boundary.

Old Church Slavonic manuscripts preserve a later South Slavic literary variety and primarily ecclesiastical texts. They illuminate ninth-century language and translation, not a verbatim record of every earlier dialect. Reconstructed Proto-Slavic forms are scholarly models built by comparison; they have no surviving sixth- to eighth-century author, manuscript, or original spelling.

Scientific comparison of sixth- to eighth-century cremations finds substantial variation in heat intensity and pyre management between sites. That diversity may reflect local ritual choices, available labor, and different sequences of collecting remains. Burned bone can reveal technique, but it cannot by itself name a deity, doctrine, or ethnic group.

In Dalmatia, cremation graves and so-called Slavic pottery are difficult to date securely before the late seventh century. They support some population movement without proving the simultaneous arrival of a named modern nation. Burial rite, object style, migration, and ethnic identity must be argued separately instead of bundled together.

Fredegar's story of Samo preserves conflict, alliance, trade, and leadership among groups called Wends or Slavs, yet its vocabulary advances a Frankish narrative. Samo's coalition was a consequential political achievement in one region. Its uncertain extent and short documentation prevent turning it into the first state of all Slavs.

Avar power structured life across much of the Middle Danube from 567 to around 800. Slavic-speaking groups could be subjects, allies, soldiers, neighbors, rebels, or communities beyond direct Avar rule. That range explains shared objects and campaigns without reducing every interaction to domination or every regional change to liberation.

By the late eighth century, Slavic settlement along the Avar realm's western edge formed part of the changing Frankish-Avar frontier. Carolingian campaigns then altered political networks. The period's achievement lies in durable communities, production, and new regional institutions, not in one empire whose borders match the atlas polygon.

ending.text: Around 800, Early Slavic communities did not disappear. The broad teaching label becomes less useful as regional settlement systems, fortified centers, elites, dialect histories, and political formations become more visible. Avar power in the Middle Danube fractured under internal change and Carolingian campaigns, while communities elsewhere followed different paths. The atlas removes proto-slavs and repaints probes as Czechs, a broad slavonic-tribes layer, the Rus khaganate, Avars, the Carolingian Empire, and later other regional polities. Two probes even have overlapping owners, demonstrating editorial layering rather than direct succession. Ironworking, farming, craft, household learning, and local identities continued through these changes. No source supports one conquest, extinction, or division into a fixed list of modern nations at 800. This card therefore records an approximate transformation with an empty successor list: it closes an analytical umbrella, not a people, language, ancestry, or shared future.
